newsitem.title: SPAIN: Pressure growing on Spain government to end strike.
newsitem.headline: Pressure growing on Spain government to end strike.

text.p: Spain's government came under increasing pressure to end an 11-day truckers' strike with taxis and service stations threatening to also stop work on Monday.
The organisation leading the strike, Fedatrans, met government representatives for a second day of negotiations on Sunday but no progress was evident.
A government official, asked by Reuters if an agreement could possibly be reached on Sunday, was skeptical.
"It's very premature. It's a long and complicated process," said the official who asked not to be named.
Development Ministry Director General of Transport Fernando Cascales did not report any progress after the morning session. The parties were meeting again after a lunch break.
"The dialogue proceeds though there is nothing definitive. We are continuing to negotiate," said Cascales, the senior official negotiating with the strikers.
Taxi drivers were threatening to join the strike on Monday, saying they want the same improvements in labour conditions and lower fuel prices which the truckers are demanding.
Service stations also plan to strike, angered by government agreement to lower fuel prices to appease the truckers.

Jose Luis Soldevilla, spokesman for the strikers, said at a news conference there were no substantial advances on their key demands for lowering retirement age to 60 from 65, recognition of professional illnesses and curbing surging fuel prices.
The strikers said they would not call off the action until there was a "true negotiation" with the government. They asked King Juan Carlos to mediate.
Foreign Minister Abel Matutes said the government would take measures to avert economic paralysis if the strike continues.
The government warned on Friday the strike was causing grave damage to the economy and prices of fish and produce could rise sharply if it lasts.
Government sources said traffic was flowing freely and there were no more blockages at the borders with France and Portugal. Few incidents of violence were reported at the weekend.
The government has ordered security escorts for trucks after the strike jammed up border crossings, cut off roads, blocked ports and disrupted the supply of goods to northern Spain.
A number of domestic and foreign carmakers and other factories were forced to cut back or stop production due to a lack of raw materials.
Spanish media reported a number of service stations in the Santander region were closed on Sunday for lack of petrol.
Civil Guards were escorting convoys of trucks when drivers requested protection against possible retaliation from strikers parked along the hard shoulders of main roads in the north.

Soldevilla said the strike committee was considering bringing criminal charges against Spanish media which reported on Sunday the Fedatrans Secretary-General Juan Miguel Abellanal was jailed for links to the violent Basque separatist group ETA and charged with robbery, kidnapping and possession of explosives.
Soldevilla said the reports were false, partial and hinted that the government was leaking the reports to the media to discredit Fedatrans.
The government blamed ETA for three deadly attacks last week including the assassination of a Supreme Court judge in Madrid.
